content: Synanon was originally established in 1958 in Santa Monica, California, by Charles Chuck Dederich Sr., a reformed alcoholic and member of Alcoholics Anonymous. Initially, it functioned as a drug rehabilitation program. By the early 1960s, it had evolved into an alternative community that emphasized self-examination and group truth-telling sessions, known as the Synanon Game. Over time, Synanon transformed into the cult-like Church of Synanon during the 1970s, but it was permanently disbanded in 1989 due to legal and financial troubles, including issues with the Internal Revenue Service. Dederich, dissatisfied with the limited support for drug addicts in Alcoholics Anonymous, created his own program to address their needs. He is credited with coining the phrase, Today is the first day of the rest of your life. In 1965, Columbia Pictures produced a film titled Synanon, directed by Richard Quine, which featured Edmond O'Brien as Dederich. Initially, Synanon operated as a two-year residential program, but Dederich later concluded that full recovery was unattainable, and thus members could never graduate. The organization also developed a successful business selling promotional items, generating approximately $10 million annually. Synanon purchased the Club Casa del Mar, a large beachfront hotel in Santa Monica, which served as its headquarters and a dormitory for drug treatment. It later acquired a large industrial building in Oakland, California, converting it into a residential facility where outsiders could also participate in the Game. Children were raised communally in the Synanon School, and juveniles were often sent there by court order. Professionals, even those without drug addictions, were encouraged to join, provided they transferred their assets to the organization. The Synanon Game was a central tool for control, functioning as a form of group therapy or social control, where members were humiliated and encouraged to expose their deepest vulnerabilities. By the mid-1970s, Synanon's practices became increasingly extreme. Women were required to shave their heads, married couples were forced to separate and take new partners, men underwent forced vasectomies, and some pregnant women were compelled to have abortions. George Lucas hired Synanon members with shaved heads as extras for his film THX 1138, and Robert Altman used them as extras in gambling scenes for his 1974 film California Split. In 1974, authorities began scrutinizing Synanon's practices and promises. The concept of lifetime rehabilitation conflicted with therapeutic norms, and allegations arose that the group was operating an unauthorized medical clinic and constructing unpermitted buildings on remote properties in California, such as Tomales Bay and Badger. Tax issues also emerged. In response, Dederich declared Synanon a tax-exempt religious organization, the Church of Synanon, but the problems persisted. Children assigned to Synanon began running away, aided by an underground railroad that sought to reunite them with their parents. Reports of beatings of opponents and ex-members, known as splittees, surfaced across the state. In 1978, a Los Angeles Grand Jury issued a scathing report condemning Synanon for child abuse and the financial benefits flowing to Dederich. Despite this, authorities were reluctant to intervene. Local media coverage was stifled by libel lawsuits from Synanon lawyers, but these lawsuits ultimately backfired, granting journalists access to internal documents. Synanon's criminal behavior escalated. On March 20, 1978, a former member was severely beaten during his honeymoon for being a splittee. A neighboring rancher who helped children escape Synanon was also attacked. In the summer of 1978, NBC aired a critical news segment on Synanon, prompting hundreds of threats from Synanon members, including letters warning of legal and physical peril. On September 21, 1978, ex-member Phil Ritter was beaten into a coma by two Synanon members, resulting in spinal meningitis. Weeks later, on October 11, 1978, two Synanon members placed a de-rattled rattlesnake in the mailbox of attorney Paul Morantz, who had successfully sued Synanon on behalf of a woman abducted by the group. The snake bit Morantz, but he survived. Dederich, in a drunken state, was arrested on December 2, 1978. Two Synanon members, including Lance Kenton, son of musician Stan Kenton, pleaded no contest to charges of assault and conspiracy to commit murder. While his associates went to jail, Dederich avoided imprisonment by formally stepping down as Chairman of Synanon. Much of the violence was carried out by a subgroup within Synanon called the Imperial Marines. The Point Reyes Light, a small weekly newspaper in Marin County, received the Pulitzer Prize for Public Service in 1979 for its coverage of Synanon, which other news outlets had avoided. Without its leader and with its reputation severely damaged, Synanon struggled to survive. The Internal Revenue Service revoked its tax-exempt status, and its properties were confiscated or sold. By the mid-1990s, the community had effectively dissolved. Despite its many faults, Synanon's program was effective for some individuals. It is credited with helping heroin-addicted jazz musicians like Frank Rehak, Joe Pass, and Art Pepper, as well as actor Matthew Stymie Beard. In 1962, Joe Pass formed a band of Synanon patients that recorded an album titled The Sounds of Synanon. Motivational speaker Florrie Fisher credited Synanon with curing her heroin addiction and promoted it in her speeches to high school students. Synanon also inspired more moderate and successful programs, such as Delancey Street, co-founded by former Synanon member John Maher. Many former members still value the positive aspects of Synanon, particularly its strong sense of community, and remain in close contact through personal relationships or online chat groups. Some even run businesses together. A branch of Synanon founded in Germany in 1971 remains operational. Synanon has been referenced in popular culture, including the Bob Dylan song Lenny Bruce from his 1981 album Shot of Love. Producer and writer J. Michael Straczynski incorporated a version of the Synanon Game into his science fiction series Babylon 5 (episode Signs and Portents). The New-Path drug treatment centers in Philip K. Dick's novel A Scanner Darkly also bear numerous similarities to Synanon.
